# Bannau Brycheiniog (Brecon Beacons) National Park

Scroll down


## Rediscover your sense of wonder

Welcome to the Bannau Brycheiniog (Brecon Beacons) National Park – 520 square miles of adventure, heritage, internationally recognised dark skies, towns, villages and nature.

Only three hours from London and an hour from Cardiff, Swansea and Newport.  Find all the information you need to reconnect with nature in the Bannau Brycheiniog (Brecon Beacons) National Park.  #Discoveryourbreconbeacons

- [breconbeaconsnationalpark](https://facebook.com/breconbeaconsnationalpark)

### [Walking , Activity](https://www.breconbeacons.org/things-to-do/walking)

Whether you prefer strolling along to take in the gems you pass or energetically stepping up a slope to get your heart pounding, you’re guaranteed to find a walk to suit your mood in the Bannau (Beacons).

[![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/Cycling-2-LR-600x400.jpg)\\
\\
Activity](https://www.breconbeacons.org/things-to-do/activities/cycling-mountain-biking)

### [Cycling and Mountain Biking , Activity](https://www.breconbeacons.org/things-to-do/activities/cycling-mountain-biking)

Cycling and mountain biking are a fabulous way to experience our glorious countryside. We have lots of different terrain to explore, including roads, towpaths, lanes and hillside tracks.

[![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/Stargazers-Winter-%C2%A9-Michael-Sinclair-LR-600x400.jpg)\\
\\
Activity](https://www.breconbeacons.org/things-to-do/activities/stargazing/10-places-to-go-stargazing)

### [Stargazing , Activity](https://www.breconbeacons.org/things-to-do/activities/stargazing/10-places-to-go-stargazing)

On a clear night in the Bannau (Beacons), you can see the Milky Way, major constellations, bright nebulas and even meteor showers. It’s enough to make anyone starry eyed.

![Special qualities](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/Maen-Llia-Matt-Botwood-LR-1920x1080.jpg)

## Special qualities

Overview

Sweeping grandeur and outstanding natural beauty observed across a variety of harmoniously connected landscapes, including marvellous gorges and waterfalls, classic karst geology with caves and sink holes, contrasting glacial landforms such as cliffs and broad valleys carved from old red sandstone and prominent hilltops with extensive views in all directions

A working, living “patchwork” of contrasting patterns, colours, and textures comprising of well-maintained farmed landscapes, open uplands, lakes and meandering rivers punctuated by small-scale woodlands, country lanes, hedgerows, stone walls and scattered settlements.

Extensive and widespread access to the Park’s diversity of wildlife and richness of semi-natural habitats, such as native woodlands, heathland and grassland, natural lakes and riparian habitats, ancient hedgerows, limestone pavement and blanket bogs including those of international and national importance.

Enjoyable and accessible countryside with extensive, widespread and varied opportunities to pursue walking, cycling, fishing, water-based activities and other forms of sustainable recreation or relaxation.

An intimate sense of community where small, pastoral towns and villages are comparatively safe, friendly, welcoming and retain a spirit of cooperation.

A sense of discovery where people are able to explore the Park’s hidden secrets and stories such as genealogical histories, prehistoric ritual sites, medieval rural settlements, early industrial sites, local myths, legends and geological treasures.

# Enjoy the beauty of the Bannau Brycheiniog (Brecon Beacons).

With mountains and moorland, standing stones and castles, lively waterfalls and vibrant communities, the Bannau Brycheiniog (Brecon Beacons) National Park has plenty to offer residents and visitors. We have a long and colourful history and a rich and varied mythology and culture. Our National Park covers approximately 520 square miles of South and Mid Wales, including parts of Powys, Carmarthenshire, Monmouthshire, Rhondda Cynon Taf and Merthyr Tydfil. It gets its name from the Central Bannau (Beacons), which dominate the skyline south of Brecon. They rise to 886 metres at Pen y Fan, the highest peak in southern Britain. Our night skies are remarkable. They’ve earned us recognition as an International Dark Sky Reserve. Our industrial heritage is magnificent: Blaenavon is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. And our rocks tell their own story. They’re so unique that a large part of our National Park has been designated a European and Global Geopark.

As a visitor to the Bannau Brycheiniog (Brecon Beacons) you are playing a key role in ensuring the area continues as a living landscape. By spending your time and money here local communities, which include those who farm the land, can thrive and in partnership with the National Park Authority, take care of this national gem.

It is named after the [Brecon Beacons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brecon_Beacons "Brecon Beacons"), or _Bannau Brycheiniog_ in [Welsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welsh_language "Welsh language"), the mountain range at its centre. This range includes the highest mountain in South Wales, [Pen y Fan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pen_y_Fan "Pen y Fan"), which has an elevation of 886 metres (2,907ft).[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brecon_Beacons_National_Park#cite_note-2) The national park has a total area of 1,344 square kilometres (519sqmi).[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brecon_Beacons_National_Park#cite_note-3) The Brecon Beacons and [Fforest Fawr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fforest_Fawr "Fforest Fawr") uplands form the central section of the park. To the east are the [Black Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Mountains,_United_Kingdom "Black Mountains, United Kingdom"), which extend beyond the national park boundary into England, and to the west is the similarly named but distinct [Black Mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Mountain_(range) "Black Mountain (range)") range. These ranges share much of the same basic geology, the southerly dip of the rock strata leading to north-facing escarpments. The highest peak of the Black Mountains is [Waun Fach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waun_Fach "Waun Fach") (811 metres; 2,661ft),[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brecon_Beacons_National_Park#cite_note-4) and [Fan Brycheiniog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fan_Brycheiniog "Fan Brycheiniog") (802.5 metres; 2,633ft)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brecon_Beacons_National_Park#cite_note-5) is the highest of the Black Mountain. The park was founded in 1957 and is the third and most recently designated [national park in Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_parks_of_Wales "National parks of Wales"), after [Snowdonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snowdonia "Snowdonia") (_Eryri_) and the [Pembrokeshire Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pembrokeshire_Coast_National_Park "Pembrokeshire Coast National Park"). It is visited by approximately 4.4 million people each year.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brecon_Beacons_National_Park#cite_note-6) ## Toponymy \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brecon_Beacons_National_Park&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Toponymy")\] The name _Bannau Brycheiniog_ is first attested in the sixteenth century, and "Brecon Beacons" first occurs in the eighteenth century as "Brecknock Beacons".[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brecon_Beacons_National_Park#cite_note-:02-7)_Bannau Brycheiniog_ derives from the Welsh _bannau_, 'peaks', and _[Brycheiniog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brycheiniog "Brycheiniog")_, the name of an early medieval kingdom which covered the area.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brecon_Beacons_National_Park#cite_note-Gomer-8) The English name is derived from the Welsh one; in the eleventh century the town of Brecon is recorded as "Brecheniauc", which became "Brecknock" and "Brecon".[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brecon_Beacons_National_Park#cite_note-9) In a paragraph on Brecknockshire, [John Leland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Leland_(antiquary) "John Leland (antiquary)")'s 1536–1539 _Itinerary_ treats the ranges between [Monmouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monmouth "Monmouth") and [Carmarthen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmarthen "Carmarthen") as a single mountain named "Black Mountain". He goes on to ascribe the name "Banne Brekeniauc" to the hills surrounding "Artures Hille" (Pen-y-Fan), also calling the range the "Banne Hilles".[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brecon_Beacons_National_Park#cite_note-10) The term "Brecknock Beacons" was used in the eighteenth century and referred to the area around Pen y Fan, which was itself was sometimes called "the (Brecknock) Beacon". For instance, Emanuel Bowen's 1729 _New and accurate map of South Wales_ labels the peak as "The Vann or Brecknock Beacon", John Clark's 1794 _General View of the Agriculture of the County of Brecknock_ refers to "the Vann, or Brecknock Beacon, the undisputed sovereign of all the mountains in South Wales", and an 1839 [tithe map](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tithe_map "Tithe map") of Cantref parish labels the mountain simply "Beacon".[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brecon_Beacons_National_Park#cite_note-11)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brecon_Beacons_National_Park#cite_note-12)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brecon_Beacons_National_Park#cite_note-13) A slightly wider definition was used in 1809 by the Breconshire historian [Theophilus Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theophilus_Jones_(historian) "Theophilus Jones (historian)"), who wrote that "of the lofty summits of the Brecknock Beacons, that most southwards is the lowest, and the other two nearly of a height, they are sometimes called Cader Arthur or Arthur's chair".[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brecon_Beacons_National_Park#cite_note-:12-14) To distinguish the Brecons Beacons range from the national park, the range is sometimes called the "Central Beacons".[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brecon_Beacons_National_Park#cite_note-Central_Beacons-15)[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brecon_Beacons_National_Park#cite_note-16) In April 2023, the national park [changed its name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brecon_Beacons_National_Park#Use_of_Bannau_Brycheiniog_in_English) to "_Bannau Brycheiniog_" in English, abandoning the previous English name _Brecon
